sentences.text: As a statement of fact the premise holds on this record: the filing itself names a limited, geographically concentrated set of foundries, subcontractors and memory makers as a risk, and says it does not make its own wafers or assemble, test or package its products.

The company's claim to have expanded supplier relationships for redundancy narrows the claim without reversing it, because adding suppliers is still dependence on outside suppliers, just on more of them.
The capex corollary fits an outsourced model, since capital spending stays under the 5% line with a margin of -2.2 points, but that room is modest and the test shows the structure, not any strain.

The inventory corollary cuts the other way: inventory outgrew revenue by +5.2 points, which does not fit suppliers acting as a binding limit in the latest quarter, though the record cannot say whether this reflects deliberate stockpiling or slack.

For the decision the step from dependence to risk is assumed rather than shown, because nothing in the record shows a disruption, and revenue grew +105.9% in the same quarter, so supply has not visibly capped results.
The claim is therefore true but mostly a standing risk-factor disclosure, and it does little to tell whether to hold an overweight position into the next report unless a supply event surfaces.
The company's own wording, a limited number and geographic concentration of suppliers across every manufacturing stage, is about as direct as the evidence for this premise can be.
The low capital intensity confirms the company has no in-house fabrication to fall back on if a foundry or packager falters.
The company says it has built redundancy and resilience into its supplier base, which weakens the reading of the claim as reliance on a narrow few.
Inventory growing faster than revenue, alongside more than doubling revenue, points to supply keeping up with demand rather than restricting it in the newest quarter.
Whether dependence becomes a cost or a constraint turns on evidence the record lacks: a supply disruption, a shortfall attributed to suppliers, or margin pressure from supplier pricing.
If inventory keeps outpacing revenue, the supplier-constraint reading weakens further; a reversal alongside slowing revenue would make it matter.

conditions.text: An 8-K reporting a manufacturing, foundry or supply disruption would turn this from a disclosed risk into a realized one.
Capital expenditure rising to 5% of revenue or more would signal a shift toward owning capacity and break the outsourced pattern the corollary tests.
Gross margin falling below 75.0% would be consistent with supplier costs or constraints biting, though the cause would need a filing to confirm it.
